example:
a1, a2, b1, b2 = Node(1), Node(3), Node(1), Node(2)
a1.next, b1.next = a2, b2
merge_sorted_lists(a1, b1)
start: Keep a finger on the head of each chain: the smaller of the two values under your fingers is the next node of the answer, so take it and move that finger on, and on a tie the first chain's node goes first. When one finger runs off the end, the rest of the other chain is already in order.

Check before you touch anything: both chains made of `Node`s with `int` values (not `bool`), never going down, with no loop, and no node shared between them, which two chains do exactly when they end on the same last node. Then splice with a dummy node and a `tail` pointer: attach the chosen head after `tail`, move `tail` and that chain on, attach whatever is left at the end, and return the node after the dummy.

start.text: The shape, with the choice and the splices left to you:
start.code:
def merge_sorted_lists(first, second):
    ...  # every check first: nothing may change on invalid input
    dummy = Node(0)
    tail = dummy
    while first and second:
        if ...:  # which head goes next? a tie goes to first
            ...  # attach first after tail, move first on
        else:
            ...  # the same for second
        tail = tail.next
    ...  # attach whichever chain is left
    return dummy.next

test_stable_identity_oracle: Every pair of sorted chains of 0 to 3 nodes with values 0 to 2, both empty included. Walking from your head must meet the original nodes in stable order, checked with `is`: for equal values, all of the first chain's nodes come before the second's. Taking the second chain's node on a tie, or building new nodes, fails here.
The walk must also reach `None` straight after the last node. Returning the dummy instead of the node after it, or not attaching the leftover part of the longer chain, both show up here.
test_rejection_precedes_mutation: `a = 1 → t` and `b = 2 → t` share the node `t`. Merging them must raise `ValueError` and leave `a.next` and `b.next` still pointing at `t`; spliced anyway, they end with `t.next = t`. Two chains share a node exactly when they end on the same last node, so compare the ends before merging.

Then each bad second argument in turn: descending `2 → 1`, the value `True`, a link to `42`, the plain int `42`, and a node whose `next` is itself. Each must raise `ValueError` with `a.next` still `t` (and the self-loop left as it was), so check both chains completely before the first link changes.
test_deep_chain: `merge_sorted_lists(None, head)` on a 10,000-node chain must return that same `head`: with one side empty, the answer is the other chain attached whole, not the dummy and not `None`. Anything recursive that follows the chain node by node, the merge or a check, goes 10,000 calls deep, and Python stops at about 1,000.

AttributeError: `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'value'` usually means the merge loop runs while one chain is already empty, as with `while first or second`. Loop while both have nodes, then attach the rest. For `42`, or a link to `42`, check `isinstance(node, Node)` first: those must raise `ValueError`.
TypeError: `'<' not supported between instances of 'Node' and 'Node'`: nodes have no order of their own, so `sorted()`, `min()` or a heap of bare nodes fails. Compare their `.value`, or sort with `key=`.
RecursionError: The deep test passes a 10,000-node chain, and Python stops recursion at about 1,000 calls. A recursive merge, or a recursive check or walk to the last node, has to become a `while` loop.

stopped: A check that walks each chain to its end never finishes on the node whose `next` is itself. Detect the loop as you walk: a set of nodes seen, or two pointers where one moves two steps and meets the other only if there is a loop.

If the merge loop never ends, the chosen chain is not moving on. After attaching `first` (or `second`) behind `tail`, advance that chain to its next node; otherwise the same node is compared and attached again, and ends up pointing at itself.

passing.text: All passing. Merge two long chains as your own input and look at the peak memory: splicing reuses the nodes, so it should stay small. If it grows with the length, something holds every node; the loop check can be two pointers, and the shared-node check needs only each chain's last node.
